title: III. Gold-Mines
paragraphs: This was the visit from Mitya that Grushenka had described to Rakitin with such horror. She'd been expecting the "message" right then, and had been much relieved that Mitya hadn't come to see her that day or the day before. She'd been hoping "please God he won't come until I've already gone," and then he'd suddenly burst in on her. The rest we already know. To get him off her hands, she'd suggested right away that he walk with her to Samsonov's, where she said she absolutely had to go "to settle his accounts," and when Mitya offered to walk her there at once, she'd said good-bye to him at the gate, making him promise to come back at midnight to walk her home again. Mitya, too, was delighted with this arrangement. If she was sitting at Samsonov's, she couldn't be off at Fyodor Pavlovitch's—"assuming she's not lying," he added at once. But from what he'd seen, he didn't think she was lying.

He was the kind of jealous man who, whenever the woman he loved was out of sight, immediately invents every sort of terrible fantasy about what she might be doing, how she might be betraying him—but the moment he's shaken, heartbroken, convinced beyond doubt of her unfaithfulness, he runs straight back to her; at the very first glance at her face, her cheerful, laughing, affectionate face, he revives instantly, casts off every suspicion, and with joyful shame curses himself for his own jealousy.
After leaving Grushenka at the gate, he raced home. Oh, he still had so much to do that day! But at least a weight had lifted off his heart.
"Now I just have to hurry and find out from Smerdyakov whether anything happened there last night, whether by any chance she went to Fyodor Pavlovitch's; ugh!" drifted through his mind.
Before he'd even reached his lodgings, jealousy had surged up again in his restless heart.

Jealousy! "Othello wasn't jealous, he was trusting," Pushkin once observed. And that remark alone shows the depth of our great poet's insight. Othello's soul was shattered, his whole view of the world clouded, simply because his ideal had been destroyed. But Othello never took to hiding, spying, peering through cracks. He was trusting, in fact quite the opposite. He had to be led on, pushed, worked up with tremendous effort before he could even entertain the idea of betrayal. That's not what a truly jealous man is like. It's impossible to picture the shame and moral degradation a jealous man can sink to without the slightest twinge of conscience. And yet it isn't as though jealous men are all vulgar, base souls. On the contrary, a man of lofty feeling, whose love is pure and full of self-sacrifice, can still hide under tables, bribe the vilest people, and grow perfectly comfortable with the lowest depths of spying and eavesdropping.

Othello was incapable of resigning himself to unfaithfulness—not incapable of forgiving it, but of accepting it as fact—even though his soul was as innocent and free of malice as a child's. It's not that way with the truly jealous man. It's hard to imagine what some jealous men can bring themselves to accept, to overlook, and what they're capable of forgiving! The jealous are the quickest of all to forgive, and every woman knows it. A jealous man can forgive with astonishing speed, though of course only after a violent scene, and he can forgive infidelity that's been all but proven, the very kisses and embraces he's witnessed with his own eyes, so long as he can somehow convince himself it's all happened "for the last time," that his rival will vanish from that day on, will go off to the ends of the earth, or that he himself will carry her away somewhere that dreaded rival can never reach. Of course, the reconciliation lasts only an hour. Because even if the rival really did vanish the next day, he'd invent another one and be jealous of him instead. And one might well wonder what kind of love needs watching over so closely, what a love could really be worth if it required such exhausting vigilance. But the jealous will never understand that. And yet there are men of noble hearts among them. It's remarkable, too, that those very men of noble hearts, crouched hidden in some closet, listening and spying, feel no sting of conscience in that moment at least, even though, with their "noble hearts," they understand perfectly well the shameful depths they've willingly sunk to.

At the sight of Grushenka, Mitya's jealousy vanished, and for an instant he became trusting and generous, genuinely disgusted with himself for his ugly feelings. But that only proved that his love for this woman held within it something far higher than he himself realized, that it wasn't merely sensual passion, wasn't just the "curve of her body," as he'd once put it to Alyosha. But the moment Grushenka was gone, Mitya began suspecting her of every low form of cunning and deceit, and felt no sting of conscience over it at all.

And so jealousy surged up in him again. In any case, he had to hurry. The first thing to do was scrape together even a small, temporary loan. The nine roubles had nearly all gone on his expedition. And, as everyone knows, you can't take a single step without money. But he'd already worked out, in the cart, where he might get a loan. He owned a fine pair of dueling pistols in a case, which he hadn't pawned until now only because he prized them above all his other possessions.

At the Metropolis tavern he'd made the acquaintance, some time back, of a young official, and had learned that this very well-off bachelor had a passion for weapons. He liked to buy pistols, revolvers, daggers, hang them on his wall, and show them off to visitors. He took great pride in them, and was quite the expert on how a revolver worked. Mitya, without a second thought, went straight to him and offered to pawn his pistols for ten roubles. The official, delighted, tried to talk him into selling them outright instead. But Mitya wouldn't agree to that, so the young man gave him the ten roubles, insisting nothing would induce him to take interest on it. They parted as friends.

Mitya was in a rush; he hurried toward Fyodor Pavlovitch's by the back way, toward the arbor, to catch hold of Smerdyakov as soon as he could. It was in this way that it later came to be established that three or four hours before a certain event, which I'll speak of later, Mitya hadn't had a farthing to his name, and had pawned an object he valued for just ten roubles, even though, three hours after that, he was in possession of thousands.... But I'm getting ahead of the story. From Marya Kondratyevna, the woman who lived near Fyodor Pavlovitch's, he learned the very unsettling news of Smerdyakov's illness. He heard the story of his fall in the cellar, his fit, the doctor's visit, Fyodor Pavlovitch's anxiety; he also heard, with some interest, that his brother Ivan had set off that morning for Moscow.

"Then he must have driven through Volovya ahead of me," Dmitri thought, but he was terribly troubled about Smerdyakov. "What's going to happen now? Who'll keep watch for me? Who'll bring me word?" he wondered. He began eagerly questioning the women about whether they'd seen anything the evening before. They understood at once what he was fishing for and reassured him completely. No one had been there. Ivan Fyodorovitch had been there in the evening; everything had gone exactly as usual. Mitya grew thoughtful. He'd definitely need to keep watch today, but where? Here, or at Samsonov's gate? He decided he'd have to keep an eye on both places, and meanwhile... meanwhile.... The trouble was he still had to carry out the new plan he'd worked out on the journey back. He was sure it would work, but he couldn't afford to delay acting on it. Mitya resolved to give it a single hour: "In an hour I'll know everything, I'll settle everything, and then, then, straight to Samsonov's first of all. I'll find out whether Grushenka's there and come straight back here, stay until eleven, then off to Samsonov's again to bring her home." That was his plan.

He flew home, washed, combed his hair, brushed off his clothes, got dressed, and went to Madame Hohlakov's. Alas, he'd pinned his hopes on her. He'd resolved to borrow three thousand from that lady. And what's more, he suddenly felt entirely convinced she wouldn't refuse him. One might wonder why, feeling so certain, he hadn't gone to her first, someone of his own sort, so to speak, rather than to Samsonov, a man he didn't even know, not of his class at all, whom he'd barely known how to address.

But the fact was that he'd never really known Madame Hohlakov well, had seen nothing of her over the past month, and knew she couldn't stand him. She'd disliked him from the start because he was engaged to Katerina Ivanovna, while for some reason she'd suddenly gotten it into her head that Katerina Ivanovna ought to throw him over and marry the "charming, chivalrously refined Ivan, with such excellent manners" instead. Mitya's manners she despised. Mitya had actually laughed at her once, and had remarked about her that she was every bit as lively and easygoing as she was uncultured. But that morning, riding in the cart, a brilliant idea had struck him: "If she's so eager for me not to marry Katerina Ivanovna"—and he knew she was practically hysterical on the subject—"then why would she refuse me the three thousand now, when it would let me leave Katya and be rid of her forever. These pampered fine ladies, once they've set their hearts on something, will spare no expense to satisfy the whim. Besides, she's rich," Mitya reasoned.

As for his "plan," it was essentially the same as before: offering his rights to Tchermashnya, though not with any commercial angle this time, as it had been with Samsonov, not trying to tempt the lady with the prospect of a six or seven thousand rouble profit, but simply offering it as security for the loan. As he worked out this new idea, Mitya was thrilled with it, though that was always how it went with him, with every new undertaking, every sudden decision. He threw himself into every new idea with passionate enthusiasm. Yet, climbing the steps of Madame Hohlakov's house, he felt a shiver of fear run down his spine. In that moment he saw, with the certainty of a mathematical proof, that this was his last hope, that if it fell through, there was nothing left for him in the world but to "rob and kill someone for the three thousand." It was half past seven when he rang the bell.

At first, fortune seemed to smile on him. The moment he was announced, he was received with remarkable speed. "As if she'd been waiting for me," Mitya thought, and no sooner had he been shown into the drawing room than the lady of the house herself came running in, announcing at once that she'd been expecting him.

"I was expecting you! I was expecting you! Though I had no reason at all to think you'd come see me, you'll admit that yourself. And yet, I did expect you. You may marvel at my intuition, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but I was convinced all morning that you'd come."

"That really is remarkable, madam," Mitya remarked, sinking limply into a chair, "but I've come to you on a matter of great importance.... A matter of the utmost importance to me, that is, madam... only to me... and I'm in a hurry—"

"I know you've come on the most important business, Dmitri Fyodorovitch; it's not some premonition, not some backward reach toward the miraculous—have you heard about Father Zossima? No, this is a matter of pure mathematics: you couldn't possibly not have come, after everything that's happened with Katerina Ivanovna; you couldn't, you couldn't, it's a mathematical certainty."
"The plain realism of everyday life, madam, that's what it is. But allow me to explain—"
"Realism indeed, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I'm entirely for realism now. I've seen quite enough of miracles. Have you heard that Father Zossima has died?"
"No, madam, this is the first I'm hearing of it." Mitya was a bit surprised. The image of Alyosha rose in his mind.
"Last night, and just imagine—"

"Madam," Mitya said, "I can't imagine anything except that I'm in a desperate position, and that if you don't help me, everything will come crashing down, me most of all. Forgive me for the crudeness of the phrase, but I'm in a fever—"

"I know, I know you're in a fever. How could you not be, and whatever you're about to tell me, I already know it in advance. I've been thinking over your fate for a long time now, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, I've been watching it closely, studying it.... Oh, believe me, I'm an experienced physician of the soul, Dmitri Fyodorovitch."

"Madam, if you're an experienced physician, then I'm certainly an experienced patient," Mitya said, making an effort to be polite, "and I feel that, since you're watching over my fate this closely, you'll come to my aid now that I'm ruined, and so allow me at least to lay out for you the plan I've come here hoping to propose... and what I'm hoping to get from you.... I've come, madam—"

"Don't explain it. That's secondary. But as for help, you're not the first person I've helped, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You've most likely heard of my cousin, Madame Belmesov. Her husband was ruined, 'come to grief,' as you so characteristically put it, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I advised him to go into horse breeding, and now he's doing splendidly. Do you know anything about horse breeding, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?"

"Not the faintest idea, madam; ah, madam, not the faintest!" Mitya cried, in nervous impatience, all but leaping out of his seat. "I'm simply begging you, madam, to listen to me. Just give me two minutes to speak freely, so I can explain the whole plan I've come here with. Besides, I'm short on time. I'm in a dreadful hurry," Mitya cried, half hysterical, sensing she was about to launch into another speech and hoping to head her off. "I've come in despair... in the very last gasp of despair, to beg you to lend me the sum of three thousand, a loan, but on the safest possible security, madam, with the most trustworthy guarantees! Just let me explain—"

"You can tell me all that afterward, afterward!" Madame Hohlakov, with a gesture, demanded silence in her turn. "And whatever you're about to tell me, I already know it all in advance; I've told you that already. You're asking for a certain sum, three thousand, but I can give you more, immeasurably more, I'll save you, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, but you must listen to me."
Mitya sprang up from his seat again.
"Madam, would you really be so kind!" he cried, overcome with feeling. "Good God, you've saved me! You've saved a man from a violent death, from a bullet.... My eternal gratitude—"
"I'll give you more, infinitely more than three thousand!" cried Madame Hohlakov, gazing with a radiant smile at Mitya's rapture.
"Infinitely more? But I don't need that much. I only need that fateful three thousand, and for my part I can offer security for that sum with infinite gratitude, and I propose a plan which—"

"Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it's settled, it's done." Madame Hohlakov cut him off, with the quiet triumph of someone doing good: "I've promised to save you, and I will save you. I'll save you the way I saved Belmesov. What do you think of gold mines, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?"
"Gold mines, madam? I've never given them a thought."

"But I have, on your behalf. I've thought about it, over and over. I've been watching you this past month. I've watched you a hundred times as you walked by, telling myself: there's a man of energy who ought to be out at the gold mines. I've studied your walk, and I've come to a conclusion: that's a man who would strike gold."
"From my walk, madam?" Mitya said, smiling.

"Yes, from your walk. You surely can't deny that character shows itself in the way a man walks, Dmitri Fyodorovitch? Science backs this up. I'm entirely for science and realism now. After this whole business with Father Zossima, which has upset me so terribly, from this very day I'm a realist, and I want to devote myself to practical usefulness. I'm cured. 'Enough,' as Turgenev says."
"But, madam, the three thousand you so generously promised to lend me—"

"It's yours, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Madame Hohlakov cut in at once. "The money's as good as in your pocket already—not three thousand, but three million, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, in no time at all. I'll make you a gift of the idea: you'll go find gold mines, make millions, come back and become a leading man, and wake the rest of us up and lead us all toward something better. Are we supposed to just leave it all to the Jews? You'll found institutions, enterprises of every kind. You'll help the poor, and they'll bless your name. This is the age of railways, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. You'll become famous, indispensable to the Ministry of Finance, which is in such a sorry state right now. The falling value of the rouble keeps me up at night, Dmitri Fyodorovitch; people don't know that side of me—"

"Madam, madam!" Dmitri broke in, with an uneasy sense of foreboding. "I shall, indeed, perhaps, follow your advice, your wise advice, madam.... I'll perhaps set off... for the gold mines.... I'll come see you about it again... many times, in fact... but right now, that three thousand you so generously... oh, that would set me free, and if you could, today... you see, I haven't a moment, not a moment to spare today—"
"Enough, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, enough!" Madame Hohlakov cut in firmly. "The question is, will you go to the gold mines or won't you—have you fully made up your mind? Answer yes or no."
"I'll go, madam, afterward.... I'll go wherever you like... but right now—"

"Wait!" cried Madame Hohlakov. And, jumping up, she ran to a handsome writing desk with a great many small drawers and began pulling them open one after another, searching for something with desperate haste.

"The three thousand," Mitya thought, his heart nearly stopping, "and right this instant... no papers, no formalities... that's how a real gentlewoman does things! What a splendid woman she is, if only she didn't talk quite so much!"
"Here!" Madame Hohlakov cried, running back to Mitya, overjoyed, "here's what I was looking for!"
It was a tiny silver icon on a cord, of the kind sometimes worn against the skin along with a cross.

"This is from Kiev, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," she went on, reverently, "from the relics of the Holy Martyr Varvara. Let me hang it round your neck myself, and with it dedicate you to a new life, a new calling."

And she actually looped the cord around his neck and began arranging it. Deeply embarrassed, Mitya bent down and helped her, and finally managed to tuck it beneath his necktie and collar, down through his shirt to his chest.
"Now you can set off," Madame Hohlakov announced, sitting back down triumphantly in her place.

"Madam, I'm so touched. I don't know how to thank you, truly... for such kindness, but... if only you knew how precious every minute is to me right now.... That sum of money, which I'll owe to your generosity.... Oh, madam, since you're being so kind, so movingly generous with me," Mitya burst out impulsively, "then let me confess to you... though, of course, you've known it for some time already... that I love someone else here.... I've been unfaithful to Katya... Katerina Ivanovna, I mean.... Oh, I've treated her cruelly, dishonorably, but I've fallen in love here with another woman... a woman you, madam, perhaps look down on, since you already know everything, but one I cannot leave under any circumstances, and so that three thousand right now—"

"Leave everything, Dmitri Fyodorovitch," Madame Hohlakov interrupted, in the most decisive tone. "Leave everything, especially women. Gold mines are your destiny, and there's no room for women there. Later, when you come back rich and famous, you'll find the girl of your heart in the very best society. She'll be a modern girl, educated, with advanced ideas. By then the dawning woman question will have gained real ground, and the new woman will have arrived."
"Madam, that's not the point, not at all...." Mitya clasped his hands, pleading.

"Yes, it is, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, it's exactly what you need, precisely what you're longing for, even if you don't realize it yourself. I'm not at all opposed to the current women's movement, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. The development of women, even their political emancipation in the near future—that's my ideal. I have a daughter myself, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, people don't know that side of me. I once wrote a letter to the author Shtchedrin on this very subject. He's taught me so much, so much about the calling of women. So last year I sent him an anonymous letter, just two lines: 'I kiss and embrace you, my teacher, on behalf of the modern woman. Keep going.' And I signed it, 'A Mother.' I thought of signing it 'A Contemporary Mother,' I hesitated over it, but I stuck with the simple 'Mother'—there's more moral beauty in that, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. And the word 'contemporary' might have reminded him of The Contemporary—a painful memory, given the censorship.... Good heavens, what's wrong?"
"Madam!" Mitya cried, finally jumping up, clasping his hands before her in helpless entreaty. "You'll make me weep if you keep delaying what you've so generously—"

"Oh, do weep, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, weep! That's a noble feeling... such a path lies open before you! Tears will ease your heart, and later on you'll come back rejoicing. You'll rush to me all the way from Siberia just to share your joy with me—"
"But please, allow me!" Mitya suddenly cried. "For the last time, I beg you, tell me, can I have the sum you promised me today, and if not, when can I come for it?"
"What sum, Dmitri Fyodorovitch?"
"The three thousand you promised me... that you so generously—"
"Three thousand? Roubles? Oh, no, I don't have three thousand," Madame Hohlakov announced, with serene astonishment. Mitya was stunned.
"But you just said... you said... you said it was as good as in my hands already—"

"Oh, no, you misunderstood me, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. If that's what you thought, you misunderstood entirely. I was talking about the gold mines. It's true I promised you more, infinitely more than three thousand, I remember all of it now, but I meant the gold mines."
"But the money? The three thousand?" Mitya exclaimed, awkwardly.

"Oh, if you meant actual money, I don't have any. I haven't a kopeck, Dmitri Fyodorovitch. I'm at odds with my steward over it right now, and I just borrowed five hundred roubles from Miüsov myself. No, no, I have no money. And you know, Dmitri Fyodorovitch, even if I did, I wouldn't give it to you. In the first place, I never lend money. Lending money means losing friends. And I especially wouldn't give it to you. I wouldn't give it to you precisely because I like you and want to save you, since all you really need is the gold mines, the gold mines, the gold mines!"
"Oh, to the devil with it!" Mitya roared, slamming his fist down on the table with all his strength.
"Aie! Aie!" Madame Hohlakov cried, alarmed, and fled to the far end of the drawing room.

Mitya spat on the floor and strode rapidly out of the room, out of the house, into the street, into the darkness! He walked like a man possessed, beating himself on the chest, on the very spot where he'd struck himself two days before, in front of Alyosha, the last time he'd seen him in the dark, on the road. What those blows on his chest meant, on that exact spot, and what he meant by them, was for the time being a secret known to no one in the world, not even told to Alyosha. But that secret meant, for him, more than disgrace; it meant ruin, suicide. That's what he'd resolved, if he couldn't get hold of the three thousand to pay off his debt to Katerina Ivanovna, and so lift from his chest, from that very spot on his chest, the shame he carried there, weighing on his conscience. All of this will be fully explained to the reader later, but for now, with his last hope gone, this man, so strong in appearance, burst into tears like a small child, just a few steps from the Hohlakovs' house. He walked on, and, not even aware of what he was doing, wiped away his tears with his fist. In this way he reached the square, and suddenly realized he'd stumbled into something. He heard a piercing wail from an old woman he'd nearly knocked over.
"Good Lord, you've nearly killed me! Why don't you watch where you're going, you scoundrel!"
"Why, it's you!" Mitya cried, recognizing the old woman in the dark. It was the old servant who waited on Samsonov, the one Mitya had particularly noticed the day before.
"And who might you be, sir?" the old woman said, in a completely different tone now. "I can't make you out in the dark."
"You live with Kuzma Kuzmitch. You're the servant there?"
"That's right, sir, I was only just running out to Prohoritch's.... But I still don't know who you are."
"Tell me, my good woman, is Agrafena Alexandrovna there now?" Mitya said, beside himself with suspense. "I walked her over there myself, not long ago."
"She was there, sir. Stayed a little while, then went off again."
"What? Went away?" Mitya cried. "When did she leave?"
"Why, right after she got there. She only stayed a minute. Told Kuzma Kuzmitch some story that had him laughing, then ran off again."
"You're lying, damn you!" Mitya roared.
"Aie! Aie!" the old woman shrieked, but Mitya had already vanished.

He ran as fast as he could to the house where Grushenka lived. At the very moment he got there, Grushenka was already on her way to Mokroe. It had been no more than a quarter of an hour since she'd left.
Fenya was sitting with her grandmother, the old cook Matryona, in the kitchen when "the captain" came bursting in. Fenya let out a piercing shriek at the sight of him.
"Screaming, are you?" Mitya roared. "Where is she?"
But without giving the terrified Fenya time to say a word, he collapsed in a heap at her feet.
"Fenya, for Christ's sake, tell me, where is she?"
"I don't know. Dmitri Fyodorovitch, dear, I don't know. You can kill me, but I can't tell you." Fenya swore and protested. "You went out with her yourself, not long ago—"
"She came back!"
"She really didn't. I swear to God she didn't come back."
"You're lying!" Mitya shouted. "I can tell from how frightened you are exactly where she is."

He tore off. Fenya, terrified as she was, felt relieved to have gotten off so lightly. But she knew perfectly well it was only because he was in such a rush—otherwise things might not have gone so easily for her. But as he ran off, he startled both Fenya and old Matryona with an unexpected move. On the table stood a brass mortar with a pestle in it, a small brass pestle, little more than six inches long. Mitya had already opened the door with one hand when, with the other, he snatched up the pestle and shoved it into his side pocket.
"Oh, Lord! He's going to kill someone!" Fenya cried, throwing up her hands.
